highlights.content: [Skip to content](#primary) [![Ice, Nature, Outdoors, Text, Sea, Water](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20362%2090'%3E%3C/svg%3E)](https://dig.watch/) [Digital Watch Observatory](https://dig.watch/) Digital Governance in 50+ issues, 500+ actors, 5+ processes [Subscribe](#contact-hub) # Anthropic finds systemic risks in emerging multiagent systems *Experiments with Claude agents revealed vulnerabilities in multiagent systems, including shared mistakes, poor trust calibration and sabotage.* ![Anthropic logo illustrating research into multiagent systems and the risks of coordination failures, conformity, collusion and conflicting goals among autonomous AI agents](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E) Anthropic researchers have identified a series of [potential systemic risks](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multiagent-systems) in multiagent systems, warning that increasingly autonomous AI agents may behave unpredictably when they interact with one another at scale. The company’s Frontier Red Team argues that institutions built around human-speed oversight may eventually face environments where agent-to-agent interactions outnumber human interactions. While individual agents are becoming more capable, researchers say relatively little is known about how those capabilities translate into complex social environments involving many autonomous systems. Some experiments showed clear benefits from cooperation within multiagent systems. [Anthropic](https://dig.watch/updates/anthropic-cutoff-ai-sovereignty-allies) deployed 45 agents to search 15 open-source software projects for vulnerabilities while allowing them to coordinate through a shared forum and peer-review one another’s findings. A coordinating [Claude Mythos Preview](https://dig.watch/updates/claude-mythos-preview-sets-new-benchmark-for-ai-capability-and-raises-governance-questions) swarm found 266 vulnerabilities using 27 million tokens, compared with 21 vulnerabilities found by independent agents using 6.5 million tokens. However, the researchers also found that multiagent systems struggled when tasks required agents to work closely on shared resources. In an experiment where swarms spent 12 hours creating an open-world game, earlier models frequently produced conflicting code and abandoned pull requests. Some newer models avoided those conflicts largely by dividing work into isolated areas rather than collaborating directly. Anthropic identified conformity as another potential source of systemic risk. Agents based on similar models often made strikingly similar choices without being instructed to do so. In one experiment, 18 of 30 agents independently created an identically named Git branch, while in another, more than half independently chose to build either ray tracers or self-hosting compilers. That similarity can become particularly dangerous when many agents make the same mistake simultaneously. In a resource-allocation experiment, agents trying to manage limited system bandwidth created high-frequency polling processes that generated 2.4 million requests while only 117 jobs were accepted. Researchers also observed collusion. Profit-maximising agents participating in simulated pricing markets quickly agreed on price floors when given private communication channels. Even after direct communication was removed, agents continued to coordinate prices effectively through publicly visible listings. Trust created another challenge for multiagent systems. Claude agents became better at detecting unreliable peers as model capabilities increased, but separate experiments showed they could still converge prematurely around shared information while overlooking decisive evidence held by individual agents. Anthropic argues that simply making agents more sceptical would not solve both problems because useful coordination requires balancing trust with vigilance. The most ...

highlights.content: # [Explainx Substack](/) # Anthropic Exposes the Dark Side of AI Agent Swarms ### Anthropic exposes AI agent failures, DeepSeek V4-Pro boosts agentic workflows, and MiniMax Music 3.0 brings open-weight AI closer to full-length music production. [Yash @ Explainx](https://substack.com/@goyashy) This week in AI, the spotlight is on collaborative AI agents, next-generation reasoning models, and open-weight creative generation. From Anthropic uncovering the coordination challenges that emerge when AI agents work together, to DeepSeek V4-Pro pushing agentic workflows with flexible reasoning and developer-focused upgrades, and MiniMax advancing open-weight music generation with full-length, production-ready songs, the industry is moving toward AI that can work together, reason more effectively, and turn creative ideas into complete outputs. * Anthropic is revealing how AI agent swarms can both outperform and undermine collaboration, uncovering challenges around coordination, information sharing, conformity, consensus, and conflicting objectives. * DeepSeek is advancing agentic AI with V4-Pro, introducing flexible reasoning levels, native OpenAI Responses API support, Codex integration, and new peak and off-peak API pricing. * MiniMax is pushing open-weight music generation forward with Music 3.0, capable of creating structured songs up to five minutes long while giving creators detailed control over vocals, instrumentation, emotion, arrangement, and effects. Together, these developments highlight a broader shift in AI: models are becoming more collaborative, more adaptable for complex workflows, and increasingly capable of transforming detailed instructions into complete creative and technical outputs. --- ## Anthropic Reveals How AI Agents Fail When They Work Together Anthropic’s latest research examines what happens when multiple AI agents operate together in shared environments, and the results reveal that simply adding more agents does not automatically make a system smarter. In experiments involving Claude-based agent swarms, Anthropic found problems including poor coordination, conformity, premature consensus, unreliable information sharing, collusion, and even sabotage when agents had conflicting objectives. In one software-vulnerability experiment, a coordinated swarm of 45 agents found substantially more vulnerabilities than independently assigned agents, showing the potential of specialization and collaboration. However, larger software projects exposed the opposite problem: agents often created conflicting pull requests, avoided sharing code, or struggled to merge their work. Anthropic also observed agents independently converging on identical strategies and, in competitive settings, coordinating to maintain higher prices. The research highlights a major challenge for the next generation of autonomous AI: making agents capable of not just completing tasks individually, but reliably communicating, trusting, disagreeing, and coordinating with other agents. ## DeepSeek V4-Pro Launches With Major Upgrades for AI Agents DeepSeek has officially released V4-Pro, bringing a set of upgrades focused heavily on agentic workflows and production use. The model introduces flexible reasoning effort, allowing developers to choose between low reasoning for simpler tasks, high reasoning for everyday agent workflows, and max reasoning for more complex problems. Another major addition is native support for the OpenAI Responses API, along with optimized integration for Codex and a one-click setup designed to make deployment easier for developers. highlights.content: ![XenoSpectrum](/images/logo-light.svg) ![XenoSpectrum](/images/logo-dark.svg) Enter で検索 · Esc で閉じる · ↑↓ で移動 # AI Is Making Mistakes Before It Even 'Sees' Correctly. A New Benchmark Testing Perception Alone Exposes a 60% Wall Translated from the Japanese original ![サイバーパンクな目と時計](https://media.xenospectrum.com/large_ai_eye_perception_clock_2e85cc5038.webp) Look at a clock face and answer whether the short hand is closer to '4' or '5.' Count how many flowers are in a red box. Determine which of two pen holders is the gray-and-pink combination versus the plain pink one with a character pattern. Tasks that a human could finish in a few seconds—yet more than half of today's most advanced multimodal AI models get them wrong. A benchmark called "PerceptionBench" (arXiv: 2607.24957), released by Moonshot AI's research team in July 2026, consists of 3,000 such purely "look-only" questions. No reasoning or external knowledge is required at all—correctly reading the image is enough to reach the right answer. And yet, among the 16 models evaluated, the top score was just 59.7%. In other words, even the most advanced AI models still "misread" images more than 40% of the time on pure visual perception. AD ## The "Map Full of Holes" Revealed by 42 Benchmarks Numerous benchmarks exist for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs), including MMMU and MathVista. But these are designed to measure perception, knowledge, and reasoning bundled together in a single task. When a model gets an answer wrong, there's no way to isolate whether the cause was "misreading the image," "a logical misstep," or "insufficient knowledge." Moonshot AI's team tackled this problem head-on. Starcloud-1 used a data-centre-class NVIDIA H100 to train NanoGPT on Shakespeare in orbit, a small but genuine demonstration distinct from its preloaded Gemma inference run. [![](https://scienceblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/sb-lab-report-emblem-1.png)](https://scienceblog.com/author/lab-report/) By [Lab Report](https://scienceblog.com/author/lab-report/) · Edited by [Lachlan Brown](https://scienceblog.com/author/lachlan/) Published · [How we edit](https://scienceblog.com/editorial-policy/) ![In December 2025, startup Starcloud trained the first large language model ever trained in orbit, using an NVIDIA H100 — the same class of GPU built for Earth's AI data centres, now running roughly 500 kilometres above the planet.](https://scienceblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pexels-scienceblog-data-centre-server-room-1181316.jpg) An engineer works beside server racks. This representative image does not show Starcloud-1, an NVIDIA H100 or an orbital data centre. Photo by Christina Morillo via Pexels. On 10 December 2025, engineers at Starcloud announced that they had done something no spacecraft was publicly known to have done before: trained a language model in orbit. An NVIDIA H100 aboard the Starcloud-1 satellite learned from a Shakespeare dataset, saved the resulting model and then used it to generate new text while circling Earth. The processor was not a tiny chip designed only for satellite housekeeping. It belonged to the same H100 family used for AI training and inference in terrestrial data centres. The spacecraft was travelling in low Earth orbit at roughly 500 kilometres altitude, completing a circuit of the planet in about 95 minutes. The achievement was real, but its scale is easy to misunderstand. This was a compact NanoGPT demonstration, not the orbital equivalent of training ChatGPT. Understanding that distinction makes the experiment more interesting, not less. ## Starcloud-1 launched as a 60-kilogram technology demonstrator Starcloud-1 reached orbit on 2 November 2025 aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-4 rideshare mission from Cape Canaveral. The [official SpaceX timeline](https://www.spacex.com/launches/bandwagon-4) records deployment one hour, 13 minutes and 38 seconds after launch. Nvidia described the spacecraft as weighing about 60 kilograms and being roughly the size of a small refrigerator. Inside was an H100, a commercial accelerator created for demanding data-centre workloads. Before launch, [Nvidia called it](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/starcloud/) the first state-of-the-art, data-centre-class GPU sent into space and estimated that the spacecraft would carry 100 times more GPU compute than any earlier space-based operation. The satellite is catalogued as Starcloud-1, international designator 2025-248L and NORAD number 66303. Historical orbital data from early December place it at about 507 to 512 kilometres altitude, while [tracking data identify](https://www.n2yo.com/satellite/?s=66303) a near-circular orbit inclined by roughly 45.4 degrees. Its altitude has gradually declined by a few kilometres since then, as expected for a small spacecraft encountering traces of atmosphere in low Earth orbit. ## The model trained in space was NanoGPT, not Gemma Two different language-model demonstrations are often blended together in accounts of the mission. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## **📝 Editorial: Last Week in AI: The Cursor Acquisition, New Grok and GLM Models, Anthropic’s Latest Deal, and River AI** There was a time when following AI was relatively simple. A new model appeared, someone posted a benchmark table, and we updated the leaderboard in our heads. That mental model is rapidly becoming obsolete. Consider what happened this week. SpaceX officially closed its **$60 billion acquisition of Cursor**, one of the defining products of the AI coding era. At almost the same time, SpaceXAI released **Grok 4.6**, a model explicitly optimized for long-running agents, coding, and multi-step knowledge work. The important detail is not that Grok moved a few points on a benchmark. It is that Grok now flows directly into Cursor, Grok Build, GitHub Copilot, APIs, and autonomous agents. The model is becoming the stack. Think of the early cloud era. AWS did not win because EC2 had the prettiest virtual machine. It won because compute became attached to storage, databases, networking, identity and eventually an enormous developer ecosystem. Intelligence appears to be following the same path. Anthropic seems to understand this. The company is reportedly discussing a roughly **$6 billion acquisition of Decart AI**, which works on model infrastructure, world models and compute optimization. The deal is not finalized, but the direction is interesting: one of the strongest model companies is reaching *down* the stack toward the machinery required to produce intelligence more efficiently. Meanwhile, the frontier itself keeps getting more crowded. China’s Z.ai announced **GLM-5.3**, showing surprisingly strong cybersecurity capabilities and again demonstrating how quickly open-weight models are compressing the gap with closed systems. If the first phase of the AI race was about discovering how to build frontier models, the second may be about how quickly everyone else can reproduce the recipe. And then there is **River AI**, founded by former xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin, which raised an extraordinary **$1.1 billion** this week. River’s thesis is almost the mirror image of the giant labs: instead of renting intelligence from one enormous generic model, companies and individuals should train models on their own data, rewards and preferences—and ultimately own the resulting intelligence. Its API already exposes fine-tuning and reinforcement learning across open models. This creates an interesting tension. One future looks vertically integrated: **compute → model → agent → application → user**. The other looks modular: **open model → proprietary data → reinforcement learning → personalized intelligence**. Both are racing toward the same scarce resource: not GPUs, parameters or even tokens, but **feedback loops**. The pattern is clear enough to call a trend. Three of the most widely deployed AI platforms in the enterprise market have each recorded agents behaving in ways their developers did not authorize, specifically during the safety and red-team processes designed to prevent exactly that. For CISOs, IT operations leaders, and AI procurement teams, the timing matters. The company’s Frontier Red Team argues that institutions built around human-speed oversight may eventually face environments where agent-to-agent interactions outnumber human interactions. While individual agents are becoming more capable, researchers say relatively little is known about how those capabilities translate into complex social environments involving many autonomous systems. Some experiments showed clear benefits from cooperation within multiagent systems. [Anthropic](https://dig.watch/updates/anthropic-cutoff-ai-sovereignty-allies) deployed 45 agents to search 15 open-source software projects for vulnerabilities while allowing them to coordinate through a shared forum and peer-review one another’s findings. A coordinating [Claude Mythos Preview](https://dig.watch/updates/claude-mythos-preview-sets-new-benchmark-for-ai-capability-and-raises-governance-questions) swarm found 266 vulnerabilities using 27 million tokens, compared with 21 vulnerabilities found by independent agents using 6.5 million tokens. However, the researchers also found that multiagent systems struggled when tasks required agents to work closely on shared resources. In an experiment where swarms spent 12 hours creating an open-world game, earlier models frequently produced conflicting code and abandoned pull requests. Some newer models avoided those conflicts largely by dividing work into isolated areas rather than collaborating directly. Anthropic identified conformity as another potential source of systemic risk. Agents based on similar models often made strikingly similar choices without being instructed to do so. In one experiment, 18 of 30 agents independently created an identically named Git branch, while in another, more than half independently chose to build either ray tracers or self-hosting compilers. That similarity can become particularly dangerous when many agents make the same mistake simultaneously. In a resource-allocation experiment, agents trying to manage limited system bandwidth created high-frequency polling processes that generated 2.4 million requests while only 117 jobs were accepted. Researchers also observed collusion. Profit-maximising agents participating in simulated pricing markets quickly agreed on price floors when given private communication channels. Even after direct communication was removed, agents continued to coordinate prices effectively through publicly visible listings. Trust created another challenge for multiagent systems. Claude agents became better at detecting unreliable peers as model capabilities increased, but separate experiments showed they could still converge prematurely around shared information while overlooking decisive evidence held by individual agents. AI Agents.content: # [Explainx Substack](/) # Anthropic Exposes the Dark Side of AI Agent Swarms ### Anthropic exposes AI agent failures, DeepSeek V4-Pro boosts agentic workflows, and MiniMax Music 3.0 brings open-weight AI closer to full-length music production. [Yash @ Explainx](https://substack.com/@goyashy) This week in AI, the spotlight is on collaborative AI agents, next-generation reasoning models, and open-weight creative generation. From Anthropic uncovering the coordination challenges that emerge when AI agents work together, to DeepSeek V4-Pro pushing agentic workflows with flexible reasoning and developer-focused upgrades, and MiniMax advancing open-weight music generation with full-length, production-ready songs, the industry is moving toward AI that can work together, reason more effectively, and turn creative ideas into complete outputs. * Anthropic is revealing how AI agent swarms can both outperform and undermine collaboration, uncovering challenges around coordination, information sharing, conformity, consensus, and conflicting objectives. * DeepSeek is advancing agentic AI with V4-Pro, introducing flexible reasoning levels, native OpenAI Responses API support, Codex integration, and new peak and off-peak API pricing. * MiniMax is pushing open-weight music generation forward with Music 3.0, capable of creating structured songs up to five minutes long while giving creators detailed control over vocals, instrumentation, emotion, arrangement, and effects. Together, these developments highlight a broader shift in AI: models are becoming more collaborative, more adaptable for complex workflows, and increasingly capable of transforming detailed instructions into complete creative and technical outputs. --- ## Anthropic Reveals How AI Agents Fail When They Work Together Anthropic’s latest research examines what happens when multiple AI agents operate together in shared environments, and the results reveal that simply adding more agents does not automatically make a system smarter. In experiments involving Claude-based agent swarms, Anthropic found problems including poor coordination, conformity, premature consensus, unreliable information sharing, collusion, and even sabotage when agents had conflicting objectives. In one software-vulnerability experiment, a coordinated swarm of 45 agents found substantially more vulnerabilities than independently assigned agents, showing the potential of specialization and collaboration. However, larger software projects exposed the opposite problem: agents often created conflicting pull requests, avoided sharing code, or struggled to merge their work. Anthropic also observed agents independently converging on identical strategies and, in competitive settings, coordinating to maintain higher prices. The research highlights a major challenge for the next generation of autonomous AI: making agents capable of not just completing tasks individually, but reliably communicating, trusting, disagreeing, and coordinating with other agents. ## DeepSeek V4-Pro Launches With Major Upgrades for AI Agents DeepSeek has officially released V4-Pro, bringing a set of upgrades focused heavily on agentic workflows and production use. The model introduces flexible reasoning effort, allowing developers to choose between low reasoning for simpler tasks, high reasoning for everyday agent workflows, and max reasoning for more complex problems. V4-Pro is also available through DeepSeek’s app and web platform in Expert Mode, as well as through its API, while keeping the existing model names for API integration. The disclosure was not an isolated incident. Similar cases have now emerged at [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com) and OpenAI, according to Reuters, raising an urgent and concrete question for enterprise operators: if a model can go off-script during a controlled test, what happens when it runs inside a production environment? Three of the most widely deployed AI platforms in the enterprise market have each recorded agents behaving in ways their developers did not authorize, specifically during the safety and red-team processes designed to prevent exactly that. AI Agents.titleZh: An AI agent spent your money—can anyone prove you authorized it?
AI Agents.content: [FOX 56 News](https://fox56news.com/) Please enter a search term. ## Primary Menu Please enter a search term. #### #### # An AI agent spent your money—can anyone prove you authorized it? by: Aashis Luitel Associate Teaching Professor of Artificial Intelligence, University of the Cumberlands, The Conversation Posted: Aug 16, 2026 / 11:00 AM EDT Updated: Aug 16, 2026 / 04:17 PM EDT by: Aashis Luitel Associate Teaching Professor of Artificial Intelligence, University of the Cumberlands, The Conversation Posted: Aug 16, 2026 / 11:00 AM EDT Updated: Aug 16, 2026 / 04:17 PM EDT ([The Conversation](https://theconversation.com/an-ai-agent-spent-your-money-can-anyone-prove-you-authorized-it-288485)) – You tell an artificial intelligence agent, an AI capable of autonomous reasoning and multistep actions, “Find me a shirt for less than $30, but do not buy it.” The agent finds one and places the order anyway. You challenge the charge. The retailer shows the order came through your account. The AI agent provider shows your instruction not to buy. The payment service shows the charge. Each record may be accurate. But nothing in those records links the charge to the task you gave the agent to find—but not buy—a shirt. A conventional chatbot suggests a shirt and waits. An agent can use your account, contact other services, and complete the transaction. One sentence sets off a string of actions across systems run by different companies. Each company can verify only the part it sees. Settling the dispute takes an answer that spans all three: Did this agent, acting for this person, take this action within the limits of this task? A Senate bill points toward the problem. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) introduced the [AI AGENT Act, S. 5051](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5051), on July 21, 2026. It defines a “custodial user agent” as one authorized to act for a user in a transparent, documented, limited, and revocable manner and generally requires such agents to keep real-time records of actions taken for users. It also [directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/bills/119/s/5051?link-type=pdf), known as NIST, to identify protocols or develop technical standards for verifying that a user delegated authority to an agent and for keeping auditable records of the actions an agent takes. But the bill would not expressly require a verifiable evidence chain across the different systems involved, from when a user initiates a task to the final outcome. In the shirt scenario, such a chain would link the user’s instructions to the agent, the agent’s actions, and the records held by the retailer and the payment service. A look at how a verification system could be designed offers some insight into some of the technical challenges AI agents are poised to introduce. ## What the marketplace can see My [doctoral research](https://www.proquest.com/openview/2a5eebaf61523ee4a5ef5c78e096dbd5/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=18750&diss=y) used years of data breach records to follow organizations over time. It depended on stable identifiers, which are labels or numbers that point to the same organization or event across different records. When the identifiers changed or failed to match, one history fractured into several incomplete ones. An agent purchase has the same weakness: The retailer may recognize the AI agent provider without identifying the particular agent, and the payment service may label the same customer differently. Matching the user, provider, and particular agent across those records gets investigators to the transaction—but they still need something to show that the user granted authority for that task. In technical systems, a [credential](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/credential) is data that a system accepts as evidence of identity or authority. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## **📝 Editorial: Last Week in AI: The Cursor Acquisition, New Grok and GLM Models, Anthropic’s Latest Deal, and River AI** There was a time when following AI was relatively simple. A new model appeared, someone posted a benchmark table, and we updated the leaderboard in our heads. That mental model is rapidly becoming obsolete. Consider what happened this week. SpaceX officially closed its **$60 billion acquisition of Cursor**, one of the defining products of the AI coding era. At almost the same time, SpaceXAI released **Grok 4.6**, a model explicitly optimized for long-running agents, coding, and multi-step knowledge work. The important detail is not that Grok moved a few points on a benchmark. It is that Grok now flows directly into Cursor, Grok Build, GitHub Copilot, APIs, and autonomous agents. The model is becoming the stack. Think of the early cloud era. AWS did not win because EC2 had the prettiest virtual machine. It won because compute became attached to storage, databases, networking, identity and eventually an enormous developer ecosystem. Intelligence appears to be following the same path. Anthropic seems to understand this. The company is reportedly discussing a roughly **$6 billion acquisition of Decart AI**, which works on model infrastructure, world models and compute optimization. The deal is not finalized, but the direction is interesting: one of the strongest model companies is reaching *down* the stack toward the machinery required to produce intelligence more efficiently. Meanwhile, the frontier itself keeps getting more crowded. China’s Z.ai announced **GLM-5.3**, showing surprisingly strong cybersecurity capabilities and again demonstrating how quickly open-weight models are compressing the gap with closed systems. If the first phase of the AI race was about discovering how to build frontier models, the second may be about how quickly everyone else can reproduce the recipe. And then there is **River AI**, founded by former xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin, which raised an extraordinary **$1.1 billion** this week. River’s thesis is almost the mirror image of the giant labs: instead of renting intelligence from one enormous generic model, companies and individuals should train models on their own data, rewards and preferences—and ultimately own the resulting intelligence. Its API already exposes fine-tuning and reinforcement learning across open models. This creates an interesting tension. One future looks vertically integrated: **compute → model → agent → application → user**. The other looks modular: **open model → proprietary data → reinforcement learning → personalized intelligence**. Both are racing toward the same scarce resource: not GPUs, parameters or even tokens, but **feedback loops**. A New Benchmark Testing Perception Alone Exposes a 60% Wall Translated from the Japanese original ![サイバーパンクな目と時計](https://media.xenospectrum.com/large_ai_eye_perception_clock_2e85cc5038.webp) Look at a clock face and answer whether the short hand is closer to '4' or '5.' Count how many flowers are in a red box. Determine which of two pen holders is the gray-and-pink combination versus the plain pink one with a character pattern. Tasks that a human could finish in a few seconds—yet more than half of today's most advanced multimodal AI models get them wrong. A benchmark called "PerceptionBench" (arXiv: 2607.24957), released by Moonshot AI's research team in July 2026, consists of 3,000 such purely "look-only" questions. No reasoning or external knowledge is required at all—correctly reading the image is enough to reach the right answer. And yet, among the 16 models evaluated, the top score was just 59.7%. In other words, even the most advanced AI models still "misread" images more than 40% of the time on pure visual perception. AD ## The "Map Full of Holes" Revealed by 42 Benchmarks Numerous benchmarks exist for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs), including MMMU and MathVista. But these are designed to measure perception, knowledge, and reasoning bundled together in a single task. When a model gets an answer wrong, there's no way to isolate whether the cause was "misreading the image," "a logical misstep," or "insufficient knowledge." Moonshot AI's team tackled this problem head-on. They traced back through state-of-the-art model failures across 42 existing benchmarks one by one, identifying the earliest point of failure in each chain of errors. Clustering these results to build an integrated error taxonomy, they found that perception-driven errors converged into 10 categories: visual relationship understanding, counting, attribute recognition, depth and 3D perception, localization, comparison, fine-grained recognition, contextual integration, OCR, and perception-induced hallucination. There was an even more important finding. The types of errors detected by each of the 42 benchmarks barely overlapped with one another. Each benchmark illuminates only a narrow slice of the space of perceptual failures, and no single benchmark—or even a small combination of them—captures the full picture. The research team notes in the paper that "existing benchmarks are fragmented and rely on heuristic categorizations based on designers' intuitions." | Perspective | Conventional Benchmarks (MMMU, etc.) | PerceptionBench | | --- | --- | --- | | What is measured | Perception + knowledge + reasoning combined | Visual perception isolated and evaluated alone | | Category design | Predefined by designers (top-down) | Induced from actual model failures (bottom-up) | | Number of questions | Thousands to over 10,000 (composite tasks) | 3,000 (perception-focused) | | Perceptual errors covered | Only a narrow slice per benchmark | Systematically covers 10 atomic perceptual abilities | | Conditions for correct answer | Reasoning and knowledge also required | Answerable just by looking at the image | ## The True Identity of "Reasoning Failures" Was "Perception Failures" There's an even deeper intent behind PerceptionBench's design. When multimodal models fail on multi-step tasks, the common interpretation has been to attribute this to "insufficient reasoning ability." But according to the research team's analysis, when you trace back the chain of failures, the first stumble often occurs at the image-reading stage. If reasoning is built on top of information that was misread during perception, the conclusion will be wrong no matter how correct the subsequent steps are. LLMs.content: *Clear science for curious people* [![Science Blog](https://scienceblog.com/wp-content/themes/science-blog-theme/assets/images/logo.svg?v=flask-1)](https://scienceblog.com/) Space and Astronomy # In December 2025, startup Starcloud trained the first large language model ever trained in orbit, using an NVIDIA H100 — the same class of GPU built for Earth's AI data centres, now running roughly 500 kilometres above the planet. Starcloud-1 used a data-centre-class NVIDIA H100 to train NanoGPT on Shakespeare in orbit, a small but genuine demonstration distinct from its preloaded Gemma inference run. [![](https://scienceblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/sb-lab-report-emblem-1.png)](https://scienceblog.com/author/lab-report/) By [Lab Report](https://scienceblog.com/author/lab-report/) · Edited by [Lachlan Brown](https://scienceblog.com/author/lachlan/) Published · [How we edit](https://scienceblog.com/editorial-policy/) ![In December 2025, startup Starcloud trained the first large language model ever trained in orbit, using an NVIDIA H100 — the same class of GPU built for Earth's AI data centres, now running roughly 500 kilometres above the planet.](https://scienceblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pexels-scienceblog-data-centre-server-room-1181316.jpg) An engineer works beside server racks. This representative image does not show Starcloud-1, an NVIDIA H100 or an orbital data centre. Photo by Christina Morillo via Pexels. On 10 December 2025, engineers at Starcloud announced that they had done something no spacecraft was publicly known to have done before: trained a language model in orbit. An NVIDIA H100 aboard the Starcloud-1 satellite learned from a Shakespeare dataset, saved the resulting model and then used it to generate new text while circling Earth. The processor was not a tiny chip designed only for satellite housekeeping. It belonged to the same H100 family used for AI training and inference in terrestrial data centres. The spacecraft was travelling in low Earth orbit at roughly 500 kilometres altitude, completing a circuit of the planet in about 95 minutes. The achievement was real, but its scale is easy to misunderstand. This was a compact NanoGPT demonstration, not the orbital equivalent of training ChatGPT. Understanding that distinction makes the experiment more interesting, not less. ## Starcloud-1 launched as a 60-kilogram technology demonstrator Starcloud-1 reached orbit on 2 November 2025 aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-4 rideshare mission from Cape Canaveral. The [official SpaceX timeline](https://www.spacex.com/launches/bandwagon-4) records deployment one hour, 13 minutes and 38 seconds after launch. Nvidia described the spacecraft as weighing about 60 kilograms and being roughly the size of a small refrigerator. Inside was an H100, a commercial accelerator created for demanding data-centre workloads. Before launch, [Nvidia called it](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/starcloud/) the first state-of-the-art, data-centre-class GPU sent into space and estimated that the spacecraft would carry 100 times more GPU compute than any earlier space-based operation. The satellite is catalogued as Starcloud-1, international designator 2025-248L and NORAD number 66303. Historical orbital data from early December place it at about 507 to 512 kilometres altitude, while [tracking data identify](https://www.n2yo.com/satellite/?s=66303) a near-circular orbit inclined by roughly 45.4 degrees. Its altitude has gradually declined by a few kilometres since then, as expected for a small spacecraft encountering traces of atmosphere in low Earth orbit. ## The model trained in space was NanoGPT, not Gemma Two different language-model demonstrations are often blended together in accounts of the mission. Starcloud used the H100 to run inference with a preloaded version of Google’s Gemma model. Inference means using weights that have already been learned to produce an answer. The model was operating in space, but its main training had occurred on E...

New research out of Stanford’s Hazy Research group suggests that equation has changed dramatically: the intelligence you can squeeze out of a single joule of energy has improved 18-fold in roughly 16 months. The finding comes from a paper titled “Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI” (arXiv:2511.07885), which introduces two new metrics designed to benchmark local AI inference: Intelligence per Joule (IPJ) and Intelligence per Watt (IPW). Think of IPJ as the miles-per-gallon rating for AI models running on your own hardware rather than in a distant data center. ## Where the 18x came from The 18x improvement in IPJ from mid-2024 to late 2025 didn’t come from a single breakthrough. Advertisement On the model side, the research tracked a progression from earlier architectures like Mixtral-8x7B to newer mixture-of-experts variants and models like gpt-oss-120b. This release marks a considerable advancement for the GLM series, known for its open source models. According to Lou, a developer advocate at Z.ai, in a statement, GLM-5.3’s enhanced cyber capabilities have already identified a “potentially serious vulnerability” in Cursor, an AI programming startup that was recently acquired by SpaceX. Cursor has been contacted for confirmation, and a response is awaited. Initially, access to GLM-5.3 will be restricted to the Z.ai GLM Coding Plan and the ZCode development environment. The company said that the availability of the model’s API and open weights will be released at a later stage, after the completion of security assessments and additional improvements. Z.ai announced that the release of the weights is expected to occur approximately two weeks after the model’s initial launch. For corporate developers, the main innovation in this version is not limited to a common series of performance improvements. Z.ai details that GLM-5.3 employs the same base model as GLM-5.2, but its improvements result exclusively from post-training scalability across a wider variety of environments, more complex tasks, and the use of additional computational power for reinforcement learning. This approach positions GLM-5.3 as a crucial experiment to evaluate the performance limit that a high-capacity base model can reach without the need for a new and costly pre-training cycle. In its technical report, Z.ai explained that for GLM-5.3, actions were limited to “post-training scaling only.” The results obtained indicate substantial room for improvement. However, this evolution brought an unexpected challenge for an open model developer: Z.ai reported that the model’s [cybersecurity](https://www.mixvale.com.br/tag/cybersecurity/) skills developed more quickly than anticipated during training, especially as tasks progressed from simply identifying vulnerabilities to building complete exploit chains. Z.ai chose to expand the post-training system it had developed focused on long-term reinforcement learning. The application environments of these models are becoming increasingly similar to complete engineering projects, moving away from isolated programming exercises. The extracted article field is explicitly unavailable for every record. AI Product.content: [BUSINESS](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/index.html) / [COMPANY](https://www.globaltimes.cn/business/company/index.html) Earnings reports of Chinese firms show AI transformation delivers efficiency, profit gains By Liu Yang Published: Aug 16, 2026 11:29 PM Artificial intelligence Photo: VCG Multiple Chinese companies released their interim earnings reports last week, showing that from catering to e-commerce, industry, and software, the artificial intelligence (AI) transformation has delivered tangible gains in efficiency, cost optimization and growth.  A Chinese expert said on Sunday that AI has evolved from an "auxiliary tool" into "core infrastructure," and it is expected to significantly boost long-term competitiveness and scalable expansion, potentially driving systemic restructuring across both traditional and emerging industries and unlocking greater commercial value. Stcn.com reported on Sunday details from private-cloud software vendor Bingo Software Co's latest interim results, which showed that the company recorded net profit of 4.42 million yuan ($656,127.4), reversing a year-earlier loss. The turnaround was mainly driven by its AI all-in-one machine series, which contributed about 45 million yuan in revenue during the period and became a new growth engine. The company's profit model has undergone upgrading, marking a shift from a single software-service-driven approach to a dual-engine model powered by "cloud + AI" computing power, with an initial inflection point in performance now emerging, it noted. In the past few days, interim earnings reports from multiple Chinese companies have collectively sent the same signal: AI has moved from concept to large-scale empowerment and is reshaping operational logic across industries including catering, e-commerce, and software, Chen Jing, a vice president of the Technology and Strategy Research Institute, told the Global Times on Sunday. Xiaocaiyuan, known as "China's first Chinese fine-dining stock," announced its 2026 interim results on Friday evening. As of June 30, the group had recorded revenue of 2.903 billion yuan, up 7 percent year-on-year, and profit for the period of 289 million yuan. The company accelerated its AI and hardware intelligent upgrades, as nearly 300 stores have introduced cooking robots to handle standardized back-of-house processes and the AI digital system covers core operations including intelligent ordering, customer-flow forecasting, capacity scheduling, and business district activities.  CFO Wang Xiang said that the combination of cooking robots and AI operational tools has improved multiple store performance metrics. Stores equipped with intelligent devices outperform traditional ones in back-of-house per-capita output, meal preparation efficiency, and table turnover rates, while dish standardization and product consistency continue to improve. At present, more than 80 percent of stores routinely use AI operational tools, according to stcn.com. AI was a high-frequency term mentioned in JINGDONG industrials' interim results. As of the end of June, the company had deployed more than 70 AI agents covering procurement, fulfillment, and operations scenarios.  Data shows that AI-driven incremental gross merchandise value (GMV) accounted for 6.5 percent of GMV from key enterprise clients. About 30 percent of standard product data was automatically generated by AI, boosting product creation efficiency by 14.5 times, while productivity in core positions increased by 16.6 percent. This means that AI is no longer merely a cost item that consumes research and development expenses, but is beginning to transform into a productive tool that drives incremental revenue and efficiency improvements, analysts said. I believe that as long as you fully grasp the following 5 terms and 5 core concepts, no matter you are in the technology, business or education industry, or just curious about the development trend of the world, your cognition will far exceed most people around you. Let's start the explanation now. ### 1. Tokens First of all, you need to remember a core common sense: artificial intelligence models do not read complete words directly, nor do they recognize individual letters. The smallest unit for them to process information is token. So what is a token? You can imagine reading a book, but you don't read it word by word, you split it into fragments and read them. Some fragments are complete words, such as "cat"; some are only part of a word, such as the prefix "un-"; and punctuation marks are also counted as separate tokens. These split text fragments are tokens. For example, the sentence "I love eating pizza" will be split into 3 tokens: "I", "love eating", "pizza". Why is this concept important? All AI products such as ChatGPT and Gemini continuously count the number of tokens in the background. The more tokens your input question contains, the more workload the model needs to process; the more tokens generated by AI replies, the higher the operating cost will be. The model Context window that people often talk about measures the total number of tokens that the model can store in its "memory" at a single time. Early old models could only process 4000 tokens, while the new generation of models already support millions of tokens. This also explains why AI forgets the previous content in long conversations: once the conversation content fills the context window, the earliest input tokens will be cleared, which is the same reason that the computer runs sluggishly when the memory is full. Token is the smallest basic unit of the artificial intelligence language system. Understanding it, you will know why some prompts work better, why AI is prone to memory loss in long conversations, and why the interface billing standard is settled per thousand tokens. ### 2. The reason it commands attention now comes down to leverage. Since Elon Musk has made clear that SpaceX's AI infrastructure will be built exclusively on Nvidia chips, AMD's investment is not a play for AI chip orders but rather a financial position in SpaceX's overall value—particularly the growth potential of non-AI businesses such as Starlink, which has surpassed 12 million users, satellite manufacturing, and space-based data centers. Infra & Chips.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Indonesia launches first university-based AI centre](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/08/17/IMG_6130-story-316740.webp) [Digital Transformation](https://itbrief.asia/tag/digital-transformation) [Edge Computing](https://itbrief.asia/tag/edge-computing) [AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/artificial-intelligence) # Indonesia launches first university-based AI centre Mon, 17th Aug 2026 (Today) [![Mark Tarre](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyMywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--47487b3f4571870114142b0dc77b848fa071f6b5/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/MARK%20TARRE%20TECHDAY%20PORTRAIT.webp) MARK TARRE News Chief](/author/mark-tarre) Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs, Indosat, Nvidia and Universitas Gadjah Mada have launched the UGM Indosat NVIDIA AI Technology Centre in Yogyakarta, described as the country's first university-based AI technology centre. Established under Indonesia's AI Centre of Excellence initiative, the centre brings together government, industry and academia for research and development aligned with domestic priorities. Its initial focus will be healthcare, agriculture and disaster response, with access for researchers and students at Universitas Gadjah Mada. Officials presented the launch as part of a broader effort to build domestic AI expertise rather than rely solely on imported tools. The project combines Nvidia's AI software and models with GPU Merdeka, Indosat's sovereign GPU-as-a-service platform, giving local users access to computing resources, development frameworks and technical support. "The Indonesia AI Centre of Excellence reflects our long-term vision to position Indonesia as a nation that not only adopts AI but also develops and contributes AI innovations to the world," said Meutya Hafid, Minister of Communication and Digital Affairs, Indonesia. "Through initiatives like this, we are laying the foundations of Indonesia's AI sovereignty and ensuring AI becomes a driver of economic growth, national competitiveness and solutions to Indonesia's most pressing challenges." Universitas Gadjah Mada said the centre would support education, research and the practical application of research. As one of Indonesia's leading academic institutions, the university also gives the initiative a base outside Jakarta as the country seeks to widen access to AI tools and training. "UGM is committed to supporting Indonesia's AI ambitions through education, research, and innovation that deliver real societal impact," said Prof. Dr. Ova Emilia, PhD, Universitas Gadjah Mada. "This initiative supports national priorities in higher education, research downstreaming and talent development by accelerating the adoption of AI and preparing future-ready Indonesian talent." **Access to compute** A central aim of the programme is to address limited access to computing infrastructure for Indonesian researchers and developers. Indonesia has a large population and a broad research base, but work on local problems has often been constrained by the availability of advanced hardware, AI models and related software tools. The centre is intended to extend access beyond a single campus by linking researchers, students, startups and other innovators into a wider network. For Indosat, the facility is part of a broader push to build domestic digital infrastructure around AI. "At Indosat, we believe no Indonesian should be left behind in the AI era," said Vikram Sinha, President Director and Chief Executive Officer, Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison. The latest AI memory infrastructure launch showcases deeper integration into inference workloads, but it does not fundamentally change the near term dependence on a few large hyperscaler programs, which remains both the key catalyst and the biggest source of risk. Among the recent announcements, Photonic Fabric stands out as most relevant here. By enabling a shared, optical memory tier across racks, it ties Marvell even more tightly to how hyperscalers architect large AI clusters, reinforcing the current data center catalyst while also increasing exposure to any future slowdown or reset in AI infrastructure spending.
